title: Modify Authentication Process: Network Provider DLL
shortTitle: Modify Authentication Process: Network Provider DLL
summary: Windows supports add-on network provider libraries so that third-party software can extend network authentication and credential management. During an interactive logon, the Winlogon module passes the user's credentials to the local notification process over a remote procedure call, and that process then distributes them in cleartext to each registered credential manager so the manager can react to the logon event. A library registered as a credential manager therefore receives the account name and password in readable form every time somebody signs in to that machine, and it is expected to return a result to the logon flow. An adversary who can add a registration entry and place a library on disk can install one that quietly stores each set of credentials while behaving normally in every other way. Because the registration lives in the registry and the library sits in a system directory, the artefacts are precise: an unfamiliar registration entry, a library that no installed package owns, and file writes from the logon notification process to unexpected locations. Servers and domain controllers see the most logons, which makes them prime targets.

beginner.definition: Windows lets extra programs join the sign-in process to handle network logons. These programs are small files called libraries. This technique means an attacker adds their own library and copies every password typed at sign-in.
beginner.whyItMatters: The sign-in process shares the typed password in plain text with these libraries. That means a fake library receives real passwords without any cracking at all. Servers and domain controllers see many logons, so one quiet change can collect a large number of accounts. Because the logon still succeeds, both users and administrators notice nothing unusual.
howItWorks: When you sign in, a Windows process called Winlogon collects your username and password.
It sends them over a local messaging interface to a helper process on the same machine.
That helper passes the password in plain text to each registered credential manager library.
Libraries are registered in the registry, so Windows knows exactly which ones to call.
An attacker adds an entry and places their own library in a system folder.
The library behaves normally but saves every password it receives into a hidden file.
beginner.example: Imagine a hotel where the receptionist tells every partner service the guest name and room key at check-in. Partners need this information to prepare the room and open the gym. Now a new partner service joins the list. The receptionist still checks guests in normally and every key still works. But the new partner writes down every name and every key in a notebook. Nobody questions it, because the receptionist simply followed the usual procedure.
takeaways: Windows hands plaintext logon credentials to registered credential managers by design.
Keep an approved list of registered network provider libraries and verify their signatures.
Unexpected registry entries in these registration keys are high priority alerts.

objectives: Explain how Winlogon and the notification helper share credentials during logon.
Describe why a registered network provider library receives plaintext passwords.
Identify the registry keys and file locations used to register these libraries.
Explain why servers and domain controllers are attractive targets for this technique.
Recommend allow listing, signature checks, and monitoring for unauthorised libraries.
